titre: CX015-2.5-3 · Computer Architecture and Operating Systems
matiere: Ch3 System Architecture · Ch4 Memory, Storage & Endianness · Ch5 Intro to OS · Ch6 Memory Management

questions.question: What can the electrical conductors of a bus physically be?
choix: Registers placed inside the processor chip itself
Wires or conductors on a printed circuit
Only optical fibres between the chips
Wireless radio links between all the components
questions.explication: The course defines bus conductors as wires or conductors on a printed circuit board.

questions.question: Which bus lines provide synchronisation and control of the bus operation?
questions.explication: Control lines coordinate the operation of the bus and of the modules connected to it.

questions.question: What is the role of the power lines of a bus?
choix: Supplying power to the components connected to the bus
Selecting which memory location will receive the data
Transporting the data words between memory and the CPU
Carrying the clock signal that synchronises every module
questions.explication: Power lines provide power to the various components attached to the bus.

questions.question: Why is the data bus described as bi-directional?
choix: It transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges
It carries data on one half and addresses on the other half
Data goes out of the CPU on a write and into the CPU on a read
The CPU and the memory can both place addresses on the bus
questions.explication: Data flows out of the CPU for a write and into the CPU for a read, so the data bus works in both directions.
questions.piege: Transferring on both clock edges is DDR double pumping, not what bi-directional means.

questions.question: Why is the address bus unidirectional?
choix: The address is always supplied by the CPU
Addresses travel only from the I/O to memory
The memory always returns the address back
It only carries read requests, never writes
questions.explication: The CPU always provides the address, so it flows one way: from the CPU to memory or I/O.

questions.question: According to the course, what is a typical data bus width for a 64-bit CPU?
questions.explication: The data bus is typically the same as, or a multiple of, the CPU word size.

questions.question: What typical size does the course give for the control bus?
questions.explication: The control bus typically has 10 to 20 lines, each with a unique purpose.

questions.question: Signals named A0, A1, A2, A3… belong to which bus?
questions.explication: A-prefixed signals are address lines.

questions.question: Signals such as /RD, /WR, CLK and /IRQ belong to which bus?
questions.explication: /RD (read), /WR (write), CLK (clock) and /IRQ (interrupt request) are typical control signals.

questions.question: What does the control signal /IRQ stand for?
questions.explication: /IRQ is the interrupt request line of the control bus.

questions.question: In terms of direction, what are the control bus signals?
choix: Always bi-directional, exactly like every data bus signal
Always input, because devices request actions from the CPU
Output, input or bi-directional depending on the signal
Always output, because only the CPU drives control lines
questions.explication: Each control signal has its own purpose, so some are outputs, some inputs and some bi-directional.

questions.question: A processor has a k-bit address bus. How many locations can it address?
questions.explication: Each extra address bit doubles the number of combinations, so k bits give 2^k addressable locations.

questions.question: When the processor is connected to memory, which register is connected to the address bus?
questions.explication: The Memory Address Register (MAR) drives the address bus; the MDR is connected to the data bus.

questions.question: When the processor is connected to memory, which register is connected to the data bus?
questions.explication: The Memory Data Register (MDR) holds the data read from or written to memory via the data bus.

questions.question: With an n-bit data bus between processor and memory, what is the word length?
questions.explication: The size of the MDR / data bus gives the size of each memory location, i.e. the word length.

questions.question: A system has an 18-bit MAR and a 16-bit MDR. What is the addressable memory in bits?
questions.explication: 262,144 locations × 16 bits = 4,194,304 bits (= 524,288 bytes).

questions.question: How many memory locations can a microprocessor using 24-bit addressing address?
A system has a 20-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. What is its addressable memory?
questions.explication: 2^20 = 1,048,576 locations × 1 byte = 1 MB.

questions.question: A system has a 16-bit address bus and 32-bit memory words. What is its addressable memory?
questions.explication: 2^16 = 65,536 locations × 4 bytes = 262,144 bytes = 256 KB.

questions.question: What characterises a point-to-point bus?
choix: It carries signals from a specific source to a specific destination
It connects buses of different bandwidths so they can communicate
It carries signals to several destinations sharing the same lines
It links the CPU to memory cards inside the same physical package
questions.explication: A point-to-point bus links one specific source to one specific destination.

questions.question: In bus terminology, what is a port?
choix: An interface unit that connects two buses with different bandwidths
A point-to-point bus for a plug-in device such as a printer
A multipoint bus that broadcasts signals to all devices on the network
A single conductor of a bus that carries one named electrical signal
questions.explication: A port is a point-to-point bus intended to connect to a plug-in device, e.g. a printer.

questions.question: What usually distinguishes a multipoint (multidrop / broadcast) bus?
choix: It needs addressing signals to identify the destination
It connects a single source to a single fixed destination
It is only used to connect a plug-in device like a printer
It can never carry data in both directions at the same time
questions.explication: Because signals go to several destinations, addressing signals identify the addressed one.

questions.question: What is a backplane (system/external) bus?
choix: A bus connecting the CPU with memory and I/O cards in the same package
A bus connecting two computers placed in separate physical buildings
A bus located inside the CPU that links the ALU and its registers
A wireless link between the motherboard and external peripherals
questions.explication: The backplane bus connects the CPU with memory and/or I/O module cards in the same physical package.

questions.question: How can buses with different capacities (bandwidths) be connected together?
questions.explication: Modern computers have several buses; buses of different bandwidths are joined by bridges.

questions.question: Why do modern computers have more than one bus?
choix: To avoid the use of control signals for synchronisation
To provide different levels of functionality and bandwidth
Because each device must have its own dedicated private bus
Because a single bus cannot carry any address information
questions.explication: A bus hierarchy separates fast and slow devices, each level offering a different functionality/bandwidth.

questions.question: In the bus hierarchy diagram, which component connects the frontside bus to main memory and the PCI bus?
questions.explication: The north bridge sits on the frontside bus and links the CPU to main memory and the PCI bus.

questions.question: In the bus hierarchy diagram, which bus links the CPU directly to the north bridge?
questions.explication: The CPU's control, address and data lines form the frontside bus going to the north bridge.

questions.question: Which three backplane buses are listed in the course?
questions.explication: The backplane buses studied are PCI, AGP and ISA.
questions.piege: ATX and BTX are motherboard form factors, not buses.

questions.question: What does PCI stand for?
questions.explication: PCI = Peripheral Component Interconnect.

questions.question: What is a bus protocol?
choix: A bridge that converts signals between two different bus speeds
A physical slot standard defining the size of expansion cards
A list of the devices currently connected to the system bus
A specification of the meaning of each bus line and its signals
questions.explication: A bus protocol delineates the meaning of each line and signal; it is an agreement on how components communicate.

questions.question: Between how many components is a bus protocol an agreement?
questions.explication: A bus protocol is an agreement between 2+ components on how they will communicate via the bus.

questions.question: On the PCI-X timeline shown in the course, which version is the most recent (around 2005)?
What do the key (notch) positions on PCI slots and adapters indicate?
choix: The bus type, PCI or ISA or AGP
The card type, graphics or network
The clock speed, 33 MHz or 66 MHz
The supported voltage, 5 V or 3.3 V
questions.explication: The key position differs between 5 V and 3.3 V slots so that an adapter cannot be inserted in the wrong voltage slot.

questions.question: Which AGP-Pro card versions are shown in the course?
questions.explication: The AGP-Pro slide shows the AGP-Pro universal, 3.3 V and 1.5 V versions.

questions.question: Which form factor is a smaller ATX variant for compact desktops, compatible with many ATX components?
questions.explication: MicroATX is a smaller ATX variant with fewer expansion slots but enough for most users.

questions.question: What characterises the EATX form factor?
choix: Designed by VIA for very low power small form factor systems
Built for slimline cases using riser cards for its expansion
Larger than ATX, with more features, slots and better cooling
Smaller than ATX, with fewer slots for compact desktop PCs
questions.explication: EATX (Extended ATX) is a larger version of ATX with extra expansion slots and more space.

questions.question: Which Intel form factor was optimised for airflow and cooling but never widely adopted?
questions.explication: BTX (Balanced Technology eXtended) was a potential ATX successor focused on airflow, but it didn't catch on.

questions.question: Which older form factors were used in slimline desktops with riser cards for expansion?
questions.explication: LPX and NLX were low-profile form factors using riser cards; they were replaced by MicroATX and Mini-ITX.

questions.question: Which are examples of server motherboard form factors?
questions.explication: SSI CEB and SSI EEB are server boards: larger, multiple CPUs, extensive RAM, enterprise reliability.

questions.question: What distinguishes server motherboards from desktop ones?
choix: Riser cards for expansion, designed for slimline low-profile cases
Support for multiple CPUs and extensive RAM, with higher reliability
Only a single CPU socket, but with integrated graphics and audio
A smaller size and fewer slots, to fit inside compact low-power cases
questions.explication: Server boards are larger, support multiple CPUs and lots of RAM, and offer enterprise-level reliability and manageability.

questions.question: According to the course, how do the motherboard components communicate?
questions.explication: Components on the motherboard communicate through the system bus.

questions.question: What is a multiprocessor system?
choix: A processor that can only execute one task at a time
A single processor that runs one program after another
A system with several buses linked through bridges
A system with two or more processors working together
questions.explication: Multiprocessors are systems with two or more processors working together.

questions.question: In Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP), how do the processors relate to each other?
choix: Peer-to-peer: every processor has fully equal access to memory
Independent: each processor runs its own separate system
Master-slave: the master controls the system, slaves do tasks
Time-shared: each processor gets the shared bus for a fixed slice
questions.explication: AMP assigns specific tasks to processors in a master-slave relationship.

questions.question: Which use cases are given for Asymmetric Multiprocessing (AMP)?
choix: Desktop office work and home multimedia use
Cloud data centres and large-scale web servers
Batch payroll and bank statement runs
questions.explication: AMP is used in embedded systems and real-time processing.

questions.question: What are the disadvantages of AMP according to the course?
choix: Unequal memory speeds and constant bus contention
Complex synchronisation and high hardware cost
Large internal fragmentation and slow booting
Limited scalability and a single point of failure
questions.explication: If the master fails, the system fails (single point of failure), and AMP scales poorly.

questions.question: What is data parallelism?
choix: Processing the data across multiple processors at the same time
Storing the same data in several caches to speed up access
Sending the data in both directions on the bus at the same time
Executing different tasks in parallel on multiple processors
questions.explication: Data parallelism splits the data across processors; task parallelism runs different tasks in parallel.

questions.question: What does SIMD stand for?
questions.explication: SIMD: the same instruction is applied to multiple data points.

questions.question: Which model executes different instructions on different data points?
questions.explication: MIMD = Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data.

questions.question: Which challenges of parallel architectures are given in the course?
choix: Higher fragmentation of the main memory partitions
Lower performance and reduced efficiency overall
Complexity in synchronisation and in data management
Inability to run more than one task at the same time
questions.explication: Benefits: performance and efficiency. Challenges: synchronisation complexity and data management.

questions.question: In which fields are modern multiprocessor systems mainly applied?
choix: Embedded sensors and basic TV remote controls
Data centres, cloud computing and HPC
Pocket calculators and simple electronic toys
questions.explication: Applications: data centres, cloud computing and high-performance computing (HPC).

questions.question: According to the course, what is the length of each memory cell?
questions.explication: Memory is a combination of cells, and each cell is 8 bits long.

questions.question: Which memories are classified as 'hybrid' in the course?
questions.explication: The hybrid category groups EEPROM, NVRAM and flash memory.

questions.question: What are the two types of RAM?
questions.explication: RAM is divided into static RAM (SRAM) and dynamic RAM (DRAM).

questions.question: Which two types are listed under ROM in the memory type list?
questions.explication: ROM: PROM and EPROM. EEPROM is listed as hybrid.

questions.question: What access time does the course pyramid give for registers?
questions.explication: Registers ≈ 1-2 ns, L1 cache ≈ 3-10 ns, L2 cache ≈ 25-50 ns.

questions.question: What access time does the course pyramid give for the L1 cache?
questions.explication: L1 cache ≈ 3-10 ns.

questions.question: In the storage pyramid, how is magnetic tape in robotic libraries classified?
questions.explication: Registers to main memory = system; fixed disk = online; optical jukeboxes = near line; tape libraries = offline.

questions.question: In the storage pyramid, how is the fixed rigid disk classified?
questions.explication: The fixed (hard) disk is online storage.

questions.question: In the storage pyramid, how are optical disks in jukeboxes classified?
questions.explication: Optical jukeboxes are near-line storage.

questions.question: What are the two types of registers mentioned?
questions.explication: Registers are either general purpose or special purpose.

questions.question: Where does the cache memory reside?
choix: Between the CPU and main memory
Between main memory and the disk
Between the bridge and ISA bus
questions.explication: Cache sits between the CPU and main memory and stores frequently used data.

questions.question: Which cache levels are supported by modern computer systems?
questions.explication: Modern systems support L1, L2 and L3 caches.

questions.question: According to the course, which memory is the only one directly accessible to the CPU, which continuously reads instructions from it?
questions.explication: Primary storage is the only one directly accessible: the CPU continuously reads and executes instructions stored there.

questions.question: In what order does the CPU access main memory?
choix: It reads the data from the cache, then sends the address to the disk
It sends the data on the data bus, then the address on the address bus
It sends the address on the address bus, then reads/writes on the data bus
It sends both the address and the data together on the control bus
questions.explication: First the memory address goes on the address bus, then data is read or written on the data bus.

questions.question: What happens to data in secondary storage when the device is powered down?
choix: It is lost, because secondary storage is volatile
It is kept only if a DRAM controller refreshes it
It is moved to the cache until the power comes back on
It is kept, because secondary storage is non-volatile
questions.explication: Secondary storage is non-volatile: data is not lost when powered down.

questions.question: How does the computer usually access secondary storage?
choix: Through the cache only, without using any input/output channel at all
Through I/O channels, using an intermediate area in primary storage
Through the ROM chip, which copies the data straight into the CPU registers
Directly from the registers, without going through main memory
questions.explication: Secondary storage is reached via I/O channels and data transits through primary storage.

questions.question: Which list matches the course's description of secondary storage?
questions.explication: Secondary storage is large, cheap, non-volatile and slow.

questions.question: In the secondary storage chain, how does each level relate to the level below?
choix: It acts as a cache of data from the level below
It stores exactly the same amount of data as it
It has no link at all with the level below it
It acts as a backup of data from the level above
questions.explication: Each level acts as a cache for the level below (registers/L1 → L2 → primary → disk → tape).

questions.question: Which type of access is associated with tape or optical (tertiary) storage?
questions.explication: Disk storage is random access; tape/optical tertiary storage is sequential access.

questions.question: Which file allocation method is fast and simplifies directory access but causes fragmentation?
questions.explication: Contiguous allocation: fast, simple directory access, but inflexible, causes fragmentation and needs compaction.

questions.question: In which file allocation method does each block point to the next, with the directory pointing to the first?
questions.explication: Linked structure: each block points to the next; good for sequential access, bad otherwise.

questions.question: Which file allocation method uses a block containing pointers to many other blocks?
questions.explication: Indexed structure: an index block holds pointers to many blocks, better for random access.

questions.question: What is the main weakness of the linked file allocation structure?
choix: It is poor for anything other than sequential access
It needs a full index block for each file stored on disk
It requires a full compaction after every file is deleted
It cannot store files larger than a single block
questions.explication: Linked allocation is good for sequential access but bad for random access.

questions.question: Which storage characteristic distinguishes location-, file- and content-addressable storage?
questions.explication: Addressability = location-addressable, file-addressable or content-addressable.

questions.question: Which storage characteristic indicates whether the memory is dynamic or static?
questions.explication: Differentiation = dynamic random access memory or static memory.

questions.question: What happens to SRAM contents if power is turned off?
questions.explication: SRAM keeps its contents only while powered; if power is lost, the contents are lost forever.

questions.question: How is DRAM content kept alive as long as needed?
choix: A DRAM controller refreshes the data before it expires
The data is copied to SRAM every few milliseconds
The bootstrap loader rewrites it regularly from the ROM chip
A UV light window on the chip recharges the cells periodically
questions.explication: The DRAM controller refreshes the data before it expires.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between SRAM and DRAM according to the course?
choix: The type of bus they are connected to
The lifetime of the data they store
The supply voltage they need to run on
questions.explication: The key difference is data lifetime: SRAM keeps data while powered, DRAM loses it in ~4 ms unless refreshed.

questions.question: How many transfers per clock can DDR2 SDRAM perform?
questions.explication: DDR performs two transfers per clock; DDR2 performs four.

questions.question: How does DDR2 double the bandwidth compared with DDR?
choix: Transferring data only on the rising edge of the clock
Multiplexing: I/O buffers run at a higher frequency than the cells
Using new memory cells that never need to be refreshed
Doubling the internal clock frequency of the memory cells themselves
questions.explication: DDR2 keeps the same cell frequency but its I/O buffers run faster and multiplex a twice-wider internal bus.

questions.question: In DDR2, how does the bus between memory cells and I/O buffers compare to DDR?
questions.explication: The internal bus from cells to buffers is twice wider than in DDR, and the buffers multiplex it.

questions.question: What access time does the course give for ROM?
questions.explication: ROM: 10-50 ns. EPROM: 45-90 ns. EEPROM: 45-200 ns.

questions.question: According to the course, what is a program for a ROM or PROM equivalent to?
choix: A page table of logical addresses
questions.explication: A ROM/PROM program is simply a multiple-output truth table.

questions.question: What characterises a PROM?
choix: Erased by shining ultraviolet light through a small window on top
Empty when manufactured, it can be permanently programmed by the user
Its contents are fixed when the chip is made and cannot change
Reprogrammed electrically while it is still inside the computer
questions.explication: PROM is blank from the factory and can be programmed once, permanently, by the user.

questions.question: How is an EPROM erased?
choix: By shining ultraviolet light through a window on the chip
By applying an electrical signal while it is in the computer
It cannot be erased once it has been programmed by the user
By removing power so the contents fade after four milliseconds
questions.explication: EPROM has a small window; UV light erases it. The window is then covered.

questions.question: Why is the EPROM window covered after reprogramming?
choix: To prevent the new contents from being erased
To protect the chip from electrical surges
To make the chip readable by the processor
To let the chip cool down after programming
questions.explication: Covering the window prevents ambient UV light from erasing the new contents.

questions.question: What access time does the course give for EPROM?
questions.explication: EPROM access time is about 45-90 ns.

questions.question: What access time does the course give for EEPROM?
questions.explication: EEPROM: 45-200 ns.

questions.question: How many bits are in a nibble?
questions.explication: A nibble = 4 bits (half a byte).

questions.question: How many megabytes are in 2 GB?
questions.explication: 1 GB = 1024 MB, so 2 GB = 2048 MB.

questions.question: How many bits are in 3 nibbles?
questions.explication: 3 × 4 bits = 12 bits.

questions.question: Which unit equals 1024 terabytes?
How many bits are in 2 KB?
questions.explication: 2 KB = 2048 bytes × 8 = 16,384 bits.

questions.question: What is endianness?
choix: The order in which bits are sent on the serial control bus
The order in which bytes are arranged within a word in memory
The order in which cache levels are searched by the CPU
The order in which processes are loaded into partitions
questions.explication: Endianness is the byte order of a multi-byte value (e.g. 16- or 32-bit integer) in memory.

questions.question: In little endian, which byte is stored at the smallest memory address?
choix: The sign byte of the whole word
questions.explication: Little endian: LSB at the lowest address.

questions.question: The value 0xA1B2C3D4 is stored in little endian from address 0x100. What is at 0x101?
questions.explication: Little endian: 0x100:D4, 0x101:C3, 0x102:B2, 0x103:A1.

questions.question: The value 0xA1B2C3D4 is stored in big endian from address 0x100. What is at 0x102?
The 16-bit value 0xABCD is stored in little endian at addresses 0 and 1. What is at address 0?
questions.explication: Little endian stores the least significant byte (0xCD) at the lower address.

questions.question: Memory holds 0x29 at address 0, 0xA4 at 1, 0x73 at 2 and 0x65 at 3 (little endian). Which 32-bit value is stored?
questions.explication: In little endian the byte at the highest address is the most significant: 65 73 A4 29.

questions.question: Memory holds 0x95 at address 4, 0x6D at 5, 0xAF at 6 and 0x42 at 7 (big endian). Which 32-bit value is stored?
questions.explication: In big endian the byte at the lowest address (0x95) is the most significant.

questions.question: Which systems are listed as big endian in the course?
choix: Intel systems, IBM and RS-232 links
questions.explication: Big endian: Motorola, IBM, TCP/IP. Little endian: Intel, RS-232, AMD.

questions.question: Which systems are listed as little endian in the course?
questions.explication: Little endian: Intel, RS-232, AMD.

questions.question: Which examples of systems supporting both endiannesses are given?
choix: Intel x86 and AMD Epyc processors
questions.explication: Some systems are bi-endian, e.g. Motorola PowerPC and SGI MIPS.

questions.question: Which statement is one of the fundamental properties summarised in the course?
choix: Well-written programs tend to avoid any locality of reference
Fast storage technologies cost more per byte and have less capacity
Slow storage technologies cost more per byte and have more capacity
The gap between CPU and main memory speed is closing every year
questions.explication: Fast storage costs more per byte with less capacity; the CPU-memory gap is widening; good programs exhibit locality.

questions.question: What does the course say about the gap between CPU speed and main memory speed?
questions.explication: The CPU-memory speed gap is widening, which motivates the memory hierarchy.

questions.question: Besides being an interface, what is the OS responsible for?
choix: Manufacturing the hardware components of the computer system
Writing the application programs used by the end users
Managing and coordinating activities and sharing the resources
Storing the bootstrap loader permanently in the ROM chip
questions.explication: The OS manages and coordinates activities and the sharing of the computer's resources.

questions.question: In the user/application/OS/hardware diagram, which layer sits directly above the hardware?
questions.explication: Order from top: user → application → operating system → hardware.

questions.question: In the layers of a computer system, who works directly on the operating-system layer?
questions.explication: End users use applications, programmers write applications/utilities, OS designers design the OS.

questions.question: In the components of a computer system, where do compilers, editors and command interpreters belong?
questions.explication: Compilers, editors and command interpreters are system programs, which sit above the OS.

questions.question: In the components of a computer system, which items are application programs?
choix: Games, Microsoft Word and an accounting application
Process management, memory management and file systems
Machine language, microprogramming and physical devices
questions.explication: Games, Word and accounting software are application programs.

questions.question: Which layers make up the hardware part in the components of a computer system?
choix: Machine language, microprogramming and physical devices
Compilers, text editors and the shell command interpreters
Application programs and the operating system
Games, Microsoft Word and the USB accounting application
questions.explication: Hardware = machine language, microprogramming and physical devices.

questions.question: What is a single-user system?
choix: A system used by one company at the most
A system that has only one hardware device
A system that runs one process per second
A system that supports one user at a time
questions.explication: A single-user system supports one user at a time.

questions.question: What are system programs?
choix: Games and office applications sold to the public
Programs written by end users for their own daily work
Programs that run only inside the hardware chips themselves
Programs that manage the operations of a computer
questions.explication: System programs manage the operations of the computer.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS function handles creation, scheduling, termination and synchronisation of processes?
questions.explication: Process management also handles deadlocks and inter-process communication.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS function deals with deadlock management?
questions.explication: Deadlock handling and process communication are part of process management.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS function lets applications create, read, update and delete files?
questions.explication: File system management provides CRUD operations on files.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Through what does the OS manage communication with devices?
questions.explication: Device management works through device drivers.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS function translates user input into appropriate commands for devices?
questions.explication: Device management translates input into device commands and manages data sent to/from devices.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS function prevents unauthorised access to system resources and data?
questions.explication: Security and access control controls who can do what with the system.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: What two forms can the OS user interface take?
questions.explication: The OS provides a command-line based or graphical user interface.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS service loads a program into memory, runs it and terminates it normally or abnormally?
questions.explication: Program execution: load, run, terminate (normally or abnormally).

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS service manages shared memory or message passing between processes?
questions.explication: Communication exchanges information between processes via shared memory or message passing.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which OS service takes measures to correct errors to ensure a consistent state?
questions.explication: Error detection detects and corrects errors to keep the system consistent.

questions.theme: Ch5 · OS core functions and services
questions.question: Which is NOT one of the five OS services listed in the course?
questions.explication: The five services: program execution, I/O operations, file system manipulation, communication, error detection.

questions.question: What did first-generation computers (1940s-1950s) use?
questions.explication: First generation: vacuum tubes and plugboards, with no operating system.

questions.question: How was a first-generation computer used, given that it had no OS?
choix: Many users shared it at the same time through terminals
Jobs were grouped in batches and run from input queues
Several programs were kept in its memory simultaneously
Each user had sole use of the machine for a set period
questions.explication: With no OS, each user had sole use of the machine for a set period of time.

questions.question: Which technology characterised the second generation (late 1950s-1960s)?
questions.explication: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes; OSs were introduced, mostly batch systems.

questions.question: Which technology defined the third generation (1965-1980)?
questions.explication: Third generation: integrated circuits and multiprogramming (MULTICS, Unix, OS/360).

questions.question: Which operating systems belong to the second generation in the course table?
questions.explication: Second generation (1955-1965): IBM's Batch Monitor, FMS (Fortran Monitor System), IBSYS.

questions.question: What does FMS stand for in the second-generation OS list?
questions.explication: FMS = Fortran Monitor System.

questions.question: Which operating systems are associated with the fourth generation?
choix: MS-DOS, UNIX, MVS, VMS and Mac OS
FMS, IBM's Batch Monitor and IBSYS
Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS
questions.explication: Fourth generation OS examples: UNIX, MS-DOS, IBM MVS, VMS, Mac OS.

questions.question: What mainly influenced fifth-generation (1990s-present) operating systems?
choix: The replacement of transistors by relays
The invention of the vacuum tube and plugboard
The introduction of punched-card batch jobs
The rise of the internet and network computing
questions.explication: The internet and network computing shaped Windows, Linux, macOS, etc.

questions.question: Which language is the only one listed for the first generation (1945-1955)?
questions.explication: First generation: assembly only, and no OS.

questions.question: Which languages are listed for the fifth generation?
choix: C, C++, Java, Python, Ruby, Go
C, Pascal, Ada and Assembly language
questions.explication: Fifth generation languages: C, C++, Java, Python, Ruby, Go.

questions.question: Which languages are listed for the second generation (1955-1965)?
choix: C, C++, Java, Python and Ruby
questions.explication: Second generation: assembly, Fortran, COBOL.

questions.question: Which OS type allows simultaneous execution of multiple programs on a single processor?
questions.explication: A multitasking OS gives each process a share of processor time on a single processor.
questions.piege: Multiprocessing means more than one processing unit.

questions.question: How does a multitasking OS run several programs on one processor?
choix: It assigns each process to a different physical processor
It loads only one program into memory at any given time
It gives each process a certain amount of processor time
It runs each job to the end before starting the next one
questions.explication: Each process gets a slice of processor time, with priorities and an order of execution.

questions.question: Which examples of multitasking OS are given?
choix: VxWorks, FreeRTOS, QNX and Embedded Linux
macOS X, Windows 2000, OS/390 and Linux
Payroll systems and monthly bank statements
questions.explication: Multitasking examples: macOS X, Microsoft Windows 2000, IBM OS/390, Linux.

questions.question: Which OS type enables multiple simultaneous users and executes programs bit by bit?
questions.explication: Time-sharing OS: multiple simultaneous users, shared resources, programs executed bit by bit.

questions.question: Which examples of time-sharing OS are given?
questions.explication: Time-sharing examples: Multics, Unix.

questions.question: Which OS type is designed to respond within a certain period of time?
questions.explication: A real-time OS must respond within a given time limit.

questions.question: Which application is an example of a real-time OS use in the course?
questions.explication: Real-time examples: scientific experiments, medical imaging, industrial control, weapons, robots, air traffic control.

questions.question: Which OS type allows more than one active user program to be stored in main memory simultaneously?
questions.explication: Multiprogramming keeps several active programs in main memory at once (e.g. Windows, UNIX).

questions.question: Which examples of multiprocessing OS are given?
choix: Multics and the early batch monitors
questions.explication: Multiprocessing examples: Windows NT, 2000, XP, Unix.

questions.question: For which kind of work is a batch OS good?
choix: Running in small embedded consumer devices
Processing large numbers of repetitive jobs
Serving many interactive users at the same time
Responding to events within strict deadlines
questions.explication: Batch systems suit large numbers of repetitive jobs, e.g. payroll, bank statements.

questions.question: In a batch OS, where are batches placed before they run?
questions.explication: Users submit jobs centrally; batches are placed on input queues where they run.

questions.question: How is a real-time operating system (RTOS) defined in the course?
choix: An OS that groups jobs into batches and runs them one after another
An OS that processes data as it comes in, typically for embedded uses
An OS that runs only on servers with several Intel Xeon processors
An OS that lets many users share one computer through terminals
questions.explication: An RTOS processes data as it comes in, typically for embedded applications.

questions.question: What are the key characteristics of an RTOS?
choix: Large memory footprint and graphical interfaces
Deterministic response times and high reliability
Many simultaneous users and bit-by-bit execution
Batch processing and no interrupts at any time
questions.explication: RTOS: deterministic response times and high reliability.

questions.question: Which are examples of real-time operating systems?
questions.explication: RTOS examples: VxWorks, FreeRTOS. Embedded OS examples: Embedded Linux, QNX.

questions.question: Which use cases are given for RTOS?
choix: Consumer electronics and home medical devices
Payroll processing and monthly bank statements
questions.explication: RTOS use cases: industrial automation, automotive systems.

questions.question: Which are examples of embedded operating systems in the course?
questions.explication: Embedded OS examples: Embedded Linux, QNX.

questions.question: What characterises an embedded operating system?
choix: Designed to serve many users at once through remote terminals
Large, general-purpose and portable to any hardware
Built to process large repetitive jobs collected in batches
Compact, efficient and specialised for specific hardware
questions.explication: Embedded OSs are compact, efficient and specialised for specific hardware.

questions.question: Which future trends for operating systems are given in the course?
choix: Security, AI integration, cloud computing, IoT support
Single-user use, no networking and command lines only
Plugboards, vacuum tubes, batch jobs and punched cards
Fixed partitions, overlays, ISA buses and AGP slots
questions.explication: Future trends: increased focus on security, AI integration, cloud computing and IoT support.

questions.question: Why does memory need to be shared?
choix: So that the CPU can bypass the cache completely
So that ROM contents can be rewritten by users
So that several processes can be in memory at once
So that only one process can run at any time
questions.explication: For several processes to be in memory, memory needs to be shared.

questions.question: What are the two goals of memory management?
choix: Give each process its own CPU, and avoid using any memory partitions
Make every program run from ROM, and minimise the number of system buses
Make it simple for programs to find space, and maximise memory use
Store all data on disk, and keep the memory completely empty
questions.explication: Goals: make it as simple as possible for programs to find space to load/execute, and maximise memory usage to reduce waste.

questions.question: What is the memory manager responsible for?
choix: Translating user input into commands for the hardware devices
Deciding which bytes of a word go at the lowest address
Tracking which parts of memory are in use and which are not
Refreshing the DRAM cells before their contents expire
questions.explication: The memory manager keeps track of used and free parts of memory so they can be allocated and deallocated.

questions.question: Which three memory management techniques are covered in the course?
choix: Single tasking with overlay, fixed and variable partitioning
Paging, segmentation and demand paging with a TLB address cache
First fit, best fit and worst fit placement policies
Contiguous, linked and indexed file allocation on the disk
questions.explication: The three techniques: single tasking with overlay, fixed partitioning, variable partitioning.
questions.piege: First/best/worst fit are allocation algorithms used inside variable partitioning.

questions.question: What is a logical address?
choix: An address seen by the memory unit
An address permanently stored in the ROM
An address generated by the CPU
An address of a disk block
questions.explication: Logical address = generated by the CPU. Physical address = seen by the memory unit.

questions.question: Into which register is the physical address loaded?
questions.explication: The physical address is loaded into the memory address register (MAR).

questions.question: Which hardware unit translates logical addresses into physical addresses?
questions.explication: The MMU (memory manager) maps the CPU's logical addresses to physical addresses.

questions.question: In the MMU diagram, how is the physical address obtained?
choix: By subtracting the logical address from the relocation register
By adding the relocation register to the logical address
By copying the logical address unchanged into the memory
By multiplying the logical address by the relocation register
questions.explication: Physical address = relocation register + logical address.

questions.question: The relocation register holds 14000 and the CPU generates logical address 356. What is the physical address?
The relocation register holds 12000 and the CPU generates logical address 450. What is the physical address?
The relocation register holds 20000 and the physical address is 20500. What was the logical address?
questions.explication: Logical = physical − relocation = 20500 − 20000 = 500.

questions.question: What does single tasking with overlay allow?
choix: The memory to be split into equal fixed-size partitions
Free memory spaces to be shuffled into one large block
Several processes to run on several processors at once
A process to be larger than the size of physical memory
questions.explication: Overlays let a process larger than physical memory run, by keeping only what is needed in memory.

questions.question: With overlays, what is kept in memory at any given time?
choix: Only the instructions and data needed at that time
Only the data, while instructions stay on the disk
All instructions and data of every waiting process
Only the operating system and none of the program
questions.explication: Only the instructions and data needed at a given time are kept in memory.

questions.question: With overlays, where are newly needed instructions loaded?
choix: Into the ROM chip, which is reprogrammed for each step
Into a new partition created at the end of the memory
Into the cache, which then replaces the main memory
Into the space occupied by instructions no longer needed
questions.explication: New instructions are loaded into the space previously occupied by instructions that are no longer needed.

questions.question: In the overlay diagram, what must remain in memory for the whole program execution?
questions.explication: The resident code must stay in memory for the duration of execution; overlays are loaded into the overlay area when required.

questions.question: In the overlay diagram, where are the overlays loaded when required by the program?
questions.explication: Overlays are loaded into the overlay area when the program needs them.

questions.question: What is the main disadvantage of single tasking with overlay?
choix: A process can never be larger than the physical memory installed
A process cannot use more memory even when more becomes available
Compaction must be run after each overlay has been loaded
Several processes must share the overlay area at the same time
questions.explication: Overlays are designed around a given amount of memory, so extra memory cannot be exploited.

questions.question: A program has a 100-byte main program, a 50-byte data area and overlays of 100, 50 and 25 bytes. How much memory do the overlays save compared with loading everything?
questions.explication: Everything = 325 bytes; with overlays = 250 bytes; saving = 75 bytes.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the simplest form of memory management?
choix: Using virtual memory with full demand paging
Compacting the whole memory continuously after each job
Dividing the memory space into partitions
questions.explication: Dividing memory into partitions is the simplest form of memory management.

questions.question: In fixed partitioning, how many processes can a partition contain?
questions.explication: Each partition may contain exactly one process.

questions.question: In fixed partitioning, what bounds the degree of multiprogramming?
choix: The width of the data bus
questions.explication: Since each partition holds one process, the number of partitions limits how many processes are in memory.

questions.question: In fixed partitioning, what happens when a partition becomes free?
choix: The partition is resized to fit the next waiting process exactly
The partition is merged with its neighbouring partitions by compaction
The partition stays empty until the system is rebooted
A process is selected from the input queue and loaded into it
questions.explication: When a partition is free, a process is selected from the input queue and loaded into it.

questions.question: In fixed partitioning, can partitions have different sizes?
choix: Yes, they can be of equal size or of different sizes
No, all partitions must always be exactly 8 MB each
Yes, but only if compaction is run beforehand
No, every partition must be the size of the OS area
questions.explication: The course shows both equal 8 MB partitions and unequal ones (4, 2, 3, 6 MB).

questions.question: Fixed partitions of 4, 2, 3 and 6 MB are available. Which is the largest process that can be loaded?
questions.explication: A process must fit in a single partition, so the largest is 6 MB.
questions.piege: Free partitions cannot be combined to hold one process.

questions.question: What happens to the partition when a process terminates in fixed partitioning?
choix: It becomes available for another process
It is permanently removed from the main memory
It is moved out to the secondary storage device
It is merged with the OS partition
questions.explication: When a process terminates, its partition becomes available for another process.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: In variable partitioning, what is done when a process arrives and needs memory?
choix: The process waits until all other processes finish
The process is split into overlays loaded one by one
A fixed partition is chosen from a predefined list
A large enough free space is searched for this process
questions.explication: The system searches for a space large enough and loads the process where space is available.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Which algorithms are used to place processes in variable partitioning?
choix: First fit, best fit and worst fit
FIFO, LRU and optimal page replacement
questions.explication: Processes are loaded using first fit, best fit or worst fit.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: What does the first-fit algorithm do?
choix: Allocates the largest available space in the whole memory
Allocates the first available space that fits the process
Allocates the smallest available space that fits the process
Allocates the last available space that fits the process
questions.explication: First fit: first space big enough.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: What does the best-fit algorithm do?
choix: Allocates the largest available space in the whole memory
Allocates the space closest to the operating system area
Allocates the smallest available space that fits the process
Allocates the first available space that fits the process
questions.explication: Best fit: the smallest hole that is still large enough.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: What does the worst-fit algorithm do?
choix: Allocates the smallest space that fits
Refuses to allocate any free space
Allocates the first space that fits
questions.explication: Worst fit: the largest available hole.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Free holes, in order: 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K. A 212K process arrives. Which hole does first fit choose?
questions.explication: The first hole ≥ 212K scanning from the start is 500K.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Free holes, in order: 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K. A 212K process arrives. Which hole does best fit choose?
questions.explication: The smallest hole ≥ 212K is 300K (200K is too small).
questions.piege: 200K is the closest size but is too small to hold 212K.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Free holes, in order: 100K, 500K, 200K, 300K, 600K. A 212K process arrives. Which hole does worst fit choose?
questions.explication: Worst fit takes the largest hole: 600K.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Free holes, in order: 300K, 150K, 500K, 130K. A 120K process arrives. Which hole does best fit choose?
questions.explication: The smallest hole ≥ 120K is 130K.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: Free holes, in order: 300K, 150K, 500K, 130K. A 120K process arrives. Which hole does first fit choose?
questions.explication: The first hole large enough is the first one, 300K.

questions.theme: Ch6 · Variable partitioning and fit algorithms
questions.question: In the variable partitioning diagram, P1 starts at 400K and P2 starts at 1000K. What is the size of P1?
questions.explication: P1 occupies 400K to 1000K, i.e. 600K.

questions.question: What is fragmentation?
choix: The division of memory into equal fixed partitions by the OS
Small pieces of memory left unused because of how spaces are used
The order in which bytes of a word are stored in the memory
The splitting of a program into overlays loaded one after another
questions.explication: Fragmentation is when memory is used so that small unusable pieces are left over.

questions.question: When does fragmentation occur naturally on a disk?
choix: When files are always stored in a single linked block
When files are frequently created, deleted and modified
When the disk is used only for reading files in order
When the disk is formatted once and never written again
questions.explication: Frequent creating, deleting and modifying of files naturally fragments a disk.

questions.question: Which type of fragmentation is caused by variable partitioning?
questions.explication: Variable partitioning leaves many small non-contiguous holes: external fragmentation.

questions.question: Which type of fragmentation is caused by fixed partitioning?
questions.explication: Fixed partitioning allocates extra space a process does not use: internal fragmentation.

questions.question: What characterises external fragmentation?
choix: The CPU-generated address differs from the one seen by memory
A process is given more space than it actually needs inside its fixed partition
A process is too large for the physical memory and therefore needs overlays
Enough total free space exists, but not contiguous, so it can't be used
questions.explication: External fragmentation: many small non-contiguous holes that cannot be allocated, even if their total is enough.

questions.question: What characterises internal fragmentation?
choix: Extra space allocated to a process that it does not use
A process that is too large to fit in physical memory
Free memory blocks shuffled together to form a big one
Small free holes scattered between the allocated processes
questions.explication: Internal fragmentation is the difference between the space allocated and the space actually used.

questions.question: Which technique is used to resolve external fragmentation?
questions.explication: Compaction shuffles all free memory spaces together to form one large block.

questions.question: What does compaction do?
choix: It splits each process into overlays to reduce its memory size
It divides memory into fixed partitions of exactly equal size
It allocates the smallest free space that will fit the process
It shuffles all free memory spaces together into one large block
questions.explication: Compaction moves processes so all free space forms one large contiguous block.

questions.question: A 188-byte process is placed in a 200-byte fixed partition. How much internal fragmentation does it cause?
questions.explication: 200 − 188 = 12 bytes wasted inside the partition.

questions.question: Free holes of 30K, 40K and 50K are scattered in memory, and a 100K process arrives. What is the situation?
choix: No problem: worst fit loads it into the 50K free hole
No problem: the process is split across the three holes
Internal fragmentation: 20K is wasted inside a partition
External fragmentation: 120K is free but not contiguous
questions.explication: The total (120K) is enough, but no single hole fits 100K: this is external fragmentation, solved by compaction.

questions.question: Why can't the small free spaces of external fragmentation be used?
choix: Because they are read-only memory areas
Because they are reserved for the OS
questions.explication: Small spaces cannot be used since they are not contiguous.
